name: Eye-level angle
camera_position: camera lens at the subject's eye height, axis level
height: subject's eye height (standing adult ~1.5-1.7 m; seated ~1.2 m; child ~1.0 m)
view: horizon passes through the subject's eyes; verticals parallel
purpose: neutral reference; equality between viewer and subject; the default that makes other angles meaningful
perceptual_effect: least perspective distortion of the face; viewer shares the subject's horizon (horizon ratio: equal-height people standing on flat ground all have their eyes on the horizon)
possible_emotions: trust: highest at eye level for direct-to-camera speakers (BaranowskiHecht2018, N=34, vs 30 deg up/down) [EVIDENCE, medium]
flat or boring when every shot uses it [CRAFT]
example_use: staff member explaining lens coatings to camera; Mint & Tao talking side by side at the same eye line
mistakes: 'eye level' set at the photographer's standing height for a seated or child subject (it becomes a high angle)
AI drift: models default to a flat eye-level camera even when another angle is asked (BernalBerdun2025-PreciseCam)
combine_with: soft frontal/45 deg key, neutral colour, centred or thirds composition; vary shot size instead of angle for rhythm
how: camera height = subject eye height; level the camera; 50-85 mm-equivalent look for faces
limits: no inherent drama; context decides the meaning

name: High angle
camera_position: above the subject's eyes, pitched down (typically 10-45 deg)
view: looks down; ground plane fills more of the frame; verticals converge downward if strongly pitched
purpose: make the subject smaller in its world, show the floor/space around it, show what lies on a surface
perceptual_effect: subject appears smaller and lower in frame; face foreshortened (forehead larger, chin smaller); more environment visible
possible_emotions: BUT higher competence, composure and sociability ratings for a TV speaker in McCain1977 (opposite direction) [EVIDENCE, low]
lower trust than eye level for a direct-address speaker (BaranowskiHecht2018: trend, p=.082) [EVIDENCE, low]
for products: least favourable only for low-motivation viewers (MeyersLevyPeracchio1992 via Sevenants) [EVIDENCE, low]
example_use: Mint alone at a big empty bus stop seen from above; a desk of frames from a slight high angle so all temples show
mistakes: using it on a sympathetic hero in a brand promo without intending diminishment
too steep on faces: eyes looking up into the lens read as pleading [CRAFT]
combine_with: large negative space and a cooler, dimmer palette for sadness; for products pair with soft top light and a clean surface
how: raise the camera 0.3-1 m above eye level, pitch down 10-30 deg; prompt 'high-angle shot looking down at ...'
limits: effect sizes small and direction context-dependent

name: Low angle
camera_position: below the subject's eyes, pitched up (typically 10-40 deg)
view: looks up; ceiling/sky behind the subject; verticals converge upward
purpose: make the subject dominant, heroic or threatening; isolate it against the sky; make a product monumental
perceptual_effect: subject appears taller, chin and jaw enlarged, nostrils visible when steep; background simplified to sky/ceiling
possible_emotions: potency/strength/dominance (Kraft1987; MandellShaw1973; SevenantsDYdewalle2006 - in story order only) [EVIDENCE, medium]
NO effect when the pictures lacked narrative order (SevenantsDYdewalle2006) and none in Meridian 1987 (cited there) [EVIDENCE, mixed]
LOWEST trust for a direct-address speaker (BaranowskiHecht2018, p=.007) [EVIDENCE, medium]
products rated more favourably by low-motivation viewers (MeyersLevyPeracchio1992) [EVIDENCE, low; replication contested]
media already depict powerful people from below more often (Giessner2011) - a learned code [EVIDENCE, medium]

credibility: only one of three newsreaders gained (communicative ability, knowledgeability) from a lower vantage point; no change in 'authoritative' (Tiemens1970 via BaranowskiHecht2018) [EVIDENCE, low]
dominance judgments of faces vary with vertical viewing angle (MignaultChaudhuri2003 via Giessner2011) [EVIDENCE, low-medium]
example_use: hero shot of sunglasses standing on a beach rock against the sky; Tao finally standing up for himself
mistakes: steep low angle on a face with glasses: nostrils, under-chin and ceiling lights reflected in the lenses
assuming it makes a talking head more persuasive (evidence says less trust)
too much empty sky pushing the head against the bottom edge
combine_with: rim/back light against a bright sky and warm saturated colour for triumph, or hard underlight for threat; keep the head pose slightly down to avoid the chin-up look (head tilt interacts: WitkowerTracy2019)
how: camera at chest/waist height of the subject, pitched up 15-30 deg; prompt 'low-angle shot from knee height looking up at ...'
limits: reinforces an existing story; weak on its own

name: Bird's-eye view
camera_position: high above the scene, looking steeply down (not necessarily straight down)
view: layout, paths and patterns visible; people become small shapes; 3-point convergence downward
purpose: show geography, crowds, maps, fate, a character's smallness in a system
perceptual_effect: the scene reads as a pattern/map; individual emotion is hard to read (small faces are read more slowly: CuttingArmstrong2016)
possible_emotions: insignificance/loneliness with one small figure [CRAFT, consistent with high-angle findings]
example_use: Hua Hin beach umbrellas from above as an intro; brand battle map clips
mistakes: called 'overhead' when it is not straight down (keep the distinction)
AI buildings leaning inconsistently (mixed VP3)
combine_with: graphic composition, strong shapes and long low-sun shadows, minimal text
how: camera 20-100 m up, pitch 45-80 deg down; prompt 'aerial bird's-eye view'
limits: no facial emotion; needs strong shape design

name: Worm's-eye view
camera_position: near the ground looking steeply up
view: sky/ceiling dominates; tall things tower; strong upward 3-point convergence
purpose: extreme scale, awe, threat, a child's or small creature's viewpoint
perceptual_effect: exaggerated height and looming; strong extension distortion when close with a wide lens
possible_emotions: the viewer feels small [DERIVED from the high/low-angle logic]
example_use: a giant shop sign looming over tiny Mint; coconut palms from below at the beach
mistakes: confused with low angle (worm's eye is extreme and ground-based)
used on products: frame shape distorted
combine_with: wide lens, sky gradient, silhouettes; low rumble SFX in clips
how: camera on the ground pitched up 45-90 deg, 16-24 mm look
limits: rarely flattering for people

name: Dutch angle (canted / tilted frame)
camera_position: any position, camera rolled around the lens axis
view: horizon and verticals tilted relative to the frame edges
purpose: signal instability, wrongness, madness, disorientation
perceptual_effect: frame edges no longer align with gravity; the viewer has to re-orient
possible_emotions: unease/disorientation [CRAFT only - no controlled study found this session]
energy in action and music videos [CRAFT]
dizzy or cheap when overused [CRAFT, anecdotal]
example_use: the moment Tao realises he lost the glasses; a horror beat in night-optic
mistakes: a tiny tilt (1-3 deg) that reads as a mistake, not intent
whole scenes in Dutch angle
tilting product packshots
combine_with: unstable light (flicker, hard shadows), dissonant colour; return to level when stability returns
how: roll 8-25 deg; in rig.js cam.move({rot: 4-8}) per GUIDE.md; prompt 'dutch angle, tilted horizon'
limits: no empirical evidence of the emotional effect; keep it to 1-2 shots

name: Overhead / top-down (flat lay)
camera_position: directly above, lens axis vertical
view: plan view, nearly orthographic; no horizon; surfaces read as flat shapes
purpose: show an arrangement on a surface: flat lays, desks, recipes, a map of a room
perceptual_effect: removes height cues; becomes graphic layout; read like a page
example_use: flat lay of three frames, cleaning cloth and case on linen; the ledger on the desk in a story clip
mistakes: slight tilt = keystoned table edges
camera/phone shadow over the set
lenses reflecting the ceiling light as white blobs
combine_with: large soft top light or window light from one side for shape; grid composition; colour blocks
how: camera exactly above, sensor parallel to the table; prompt 'top-down flat lay, shot from directly above'
limits: glasses lose their face-fit context

name: Ground-level shot
camera_position: camera resting on or just above the ground, axis roughly level
view: horizon very low; ground texture in the foreground; feet, wheels and floor objects visible
purpose: show what is on the ground; intimacy with small things; a pet/child/object viewpoint
perceptual_effect: the foreground ground plane is strongly foreshortened; strong depth from the texture gradient
example_use: dropped glasses on the floor while feet walk past; sand-level beach shot with sunglasses
mistakes: calling it worm's-eye (that one looks up)
everything but the ground out of focus without intent
combine_with: shallow DOF to blur the near ground; low raking sun for texture
how: camera on the floor, roughly level; prompt 'ground-level shot, camera on the floor'
limits: limited use per story

name: Point-of-view (POV) shot
camera_position: at a character's eye position, seeing what they see
view: subjective view; no character visible (or only hands)
purpose: put the viewer in the character's head; reveal what they notice
perceptual_effect: the viewer takes the character's spatial position; often handheld drift or vision effects (blur for myopia)
possible_emotions: in our eyesight stories: experiencing blurred vs clear vision [DERIVED]
example_use: blurry street seen without glasses, then sharp after - the core eyesight-story shot; a peephole fisheye POV
mistakes: POV height not matching the character (a child's POV at adult height)
no preceding look shot, so viewers do not know whose POV it is
combine_with: sandwich look -> POV -> reaction (StudioBinder); defocus to simulate refractive error; fisheye for peepholes
how: camera at the character's eye, ~35-50 mm look; in rig.js hide the character layer, drift on
limits: needs the look/reaction context

name: Over-the-shoulder (OTS)
camera_position: behind and to one side of character A, framing B
view: A's shoulder/back of head in the foreground; B faces the camera
purpose: dialogue coverage, connection, the spatial relation between speakers
perceptual_effect: foreground occlusion adds depth; the viewer shares A's position
possible_emotions: confrontation when A's shoulder is large and dark [CRAFT]
example_use: Mint (back, foreground) listening to Tao (facing) in a dialogue carousel
mistakes: crossing the 180-degree line between OTS pairs
foreground shoulder too sharp and bright, stealing attention
combine_with: foreground darker and blurred; consistent eyelines; pair with the matching reverse OTS
how: camera behind A, A's shoulder ~1/3 of the frame; in rig.js foreground layer --d:1.3
limits: needs two characters and line discipline

name: Reverse shot (shot / reverse shot)
camera_position: the opposite camera position to the preceding shot (~180 deg turn, same side of the action line)
view: shows the other side of the exchange
purpose: alternate speakers or show what a character faces
perceptual_effect: builds a mental map of two positions; eyelines must match across the cut
example_use: Mint's MCU -> reverse MCU of Tao as he answers
mistakes: jumping the 180-degree line so both look the same way
mismatched sizes between paired shots without purpose
combine_with: matched sizes and lens looks for equality; unmatched (bigger/higher one) for a power imbalance
how: mirror the first set-up across the line of action
limits: a grammar device, not emotional by itself

name: Insert shot
camera_position: close to an object or detail within the scene
view: the object fills ~60% of the frame
purpose: give information the plot needs: a price tag, a hinge, a letter, a cracked lens
perceptual_effect: focused attention; with no face the object carries the meaning
possible_emotions: dread when the detail is a clue [CRAFT]
example_use: macro of the TR90 hinge flexing; the date in the ledger; a cracked lens on the floor
mistakes: too short to read (GUIDE.md: >= 2.5 s for short text)
insert lit differently from the master shot
combine_with: match the scene's light direction; shallow DOF; a sound accent
how: separate shot, object fills ~60%; 100 mm macro look
limits: must belong to the scene's time and space

name: Cutaway
camera_position: anywhere outside the current main action
view: something other than the main action, then back
purpose: control pace, cover edits/jump cuts, add context or a comic aside
perceptual_effect: interrupts continuity; the viewer accepts elapsed or removed time
example_use: staff talking -> cutaway to the display wall -> back (hides a cut in the talk)
mistakes: cutaway in a different look (light/colour)
so many cutaways that the main line dilutes
combine_with: same grade, sound bed continuing underneath
how: shoot 3-5 neutral details per location as B-roll
limits: no emotion of its own

name: Reaction shot
camera_position: on the listener/witness rather than the speaker
view: the face/body of the one reacting
purpose: tell the viewer how to feel about what was said or seen
perceptual_effect: the listener's expression guides interpretation (Kuleshov; curriculum ch. 11)
possible_emotions: empathy when the face carries an emotion: sad close-ups increased affective mental-state attribution, neutral close-ups did not (RooneyBalint2018) [EVIDENCE, medium]
example_use: Tao's face when Mint reads the eye-test result; for faceless Mint & Tao the reaction is carried by posture and props
mistakes: held too briefly to read (faces need size and time: CuttingArmstrong2016)
a neutral face held as a 'reaction' (does nothing per RooneyBalint2018)
combine_with: closest shot for the biggest line (GUIDE.md); soft key; silence or a sound beat
how: MCU/CU of the listener, held 1-2 s
limits: needs a readable emotional signal

name: Establishing shot
camera_position: a wide position showing the whole location
view: the full location, time of day, who is where
purpose: orient the viewer in space and time at the start of a scene
perceptual_effect: builds the spatial map that later shots rely on; long scales get longer durations in films (~8 s mean for ELS: CuttingArmstrong2016)
possible_emotions: loneliness or awe depending on scale [CRAFT]
example_use: the front of the TIME OPTIC shop at golden hour before a story starts
mistakes: skipping it so later OTS/POV shots confuse
establishing shot that does not match later interiors (weather/time)
combine_with: deep focus (hyperfocal: 24 mm f/8 -> sharp from 1.2 m to infinity), atmospheric perspective for depth
how: wide, deep focus, hold 1.5-3 s in short-form
limits: slow for short-form; 1.5-3 s in Reels

name: Extreme wide shot (EWS / ELS)
camera_position: camera on the subject's axis at the distance that gives this framing
height: usually eye level unless an angle is combined
view: landscape or whole place; people tiny
purpose: where/when, scale, isolation
perceptual_effect: shot scale = size of the focal subject in the frame; smaller faces are read more slowly and need longer shots, especially in clutter (CuttingArmstrong2016)
possible_emotions: faces unreadable; emotion read slowest at long scales (CuttingArmstrong2016) [EVIDENCE]
example_use: Hua Hin beach at dawn with one tiny figure
mistakes: faces too small to read; cut too short
definitions vary between textbooks - name the frame line (e.g. 'knees up') in prompts and shot lists
combine_with: negative space, atmosphere, horizon on a third
how: hold longer than close shots
limits: scale meanings are CRAFT conventions; the evidence covers reading speed and empathy, not fixed emotions

name: Wide / long shot (WS / LS)
camera_position: camera on the subject's axis at the distance that gives this framing
height: usually eye level unless an angle is combined
view: full bodies plus surroundings
purpose: geography, staging, who is where
perceptual_effect: shot scale = size of the focal subject in the frame; smaller faces are read more slowly and need longer shots, especially in clutter (CuttingArmstrong2016)
example_use: Mint and Tao inside the shop with the counter visible
mistakes: clutter hiding the subject (clutter slows reading: CuttingArmstrong2016)
definitions vary between textbooks - name the frame line (e.g. 'knees up') in prompts and shot lists
combine_with: clear figure-ground separation, leading lines
how: separate the subject by value/colour
limits: scale meanings are CRAFT conventions; the evidence covers reading speed and empathy, not fixed emotions

name: Full shot (FS)
camera_position: camera on the subject's axis at the distance that gives this framing
height: usually eye level unless an angle is combined
view: one body head to toe fills the frame height
purpose: body language, walking, outfit
perceptual_effect: shot scale = size of the focal subject in the frame; smaller faces are read more slowly and need longer shots, especially in clutter (CuttingArmstrong2016)
example_use: customer turning at the mirror, outfit + glasses
mistakes: cutting off the feet
definitions vary between textbooks - name the frame line (e.g. 'knees up') in prompts and shot lists
combine_with: 3/4 body angle
how: small head- and footroom
limits: scale meanings are CRAFT conventions; the evidence covers reading speed and empathy, not fixed emotions

name: Medium wide / medium long shot (MWS / MLS)
camera_position: camera on the subject's axis at the distance that gives this framing
height: usually eye level unless an angle is combined
view: knees up (frame ends near the knees)
purpose: gesture plus some setting
perceptual_effect: shot scale = size of the focal subject in the frame; smaller faces are read more slowly and need longer shots, especially in clutter (CuttingArmstrong2016)
example_use: staff handing a case to a customer
mistakes: cutting exactly at the knee joint (crop between joints)
definitions vary between textbooks - name the frame line (e.g. 'knees up') in prompts and shot lists
combine_with: two-shots in dialogue
how: frame between joints
limits: scale meanings are CRAFT conventions; the evidence covers reading speed and empathy, not fixed emotions

name: Cowboy / American shot
camera_position: camera on the subject's axis at the distance that gives this framing
height: usually eye level unless an angle is combined
view: mid-thigh up (the holster line in Westerns)
purpose: stance plus hands at hip level
perceptual_effect: shot scale = size of the focal subject in the frame; smaller faces are read more slowly and need longer shots, especially in clutter (CuttingArmstrong2016)
example_use: stylised promo pose, hand at the hip holding sunglasses
mistakes: using it with no hip-level action (MS would do)
definitions vary between textbooks - name the frame line (e.g. 'knees up') in prompts and shot lists
combine_with: low angle for a heroic stance
how: frame at mid-thigh
limits: scale meanings are CRAFT conventions; the evidence covers reading speed and empathy, not fixed emotions

name: Medium shot (MS)
camera_position: camera on the subject's axis at the distance that gives this framing
height: usually eye level unless an angle is combined
view: waist up
purpose: normal dialogue, gestures, product in hand
perceptual_effect: shot scale = size of the focal subject in the frame; smaller faces are read more slowly and need longer shots, especially in clutter (CuttingArmstrong2016)
example_use: staff explaining while holding the frame
mistakes: too much headroom
definitions vary between textbooks - name the frame line (e.g. 'knees up') in prompts and shot lists
combine_with: eye level, rule of thirds, look room
how: eyes on the upper third
limits: scale meanings are CRAFT conventions; the evidence covers reading speed and empathy, not fixed emotions

name: Medium close-up (MCU)
camera_position: camera on the subject's axis at the distance that gives this framing
height: usually eye level unless an angle is combined
view: chest up
purpose: most talking lines and reactions; face + glasses with shoulders
perceptual_effect: shot scale = size of the focal subject in the frame; smaller faces are read more slowly and need longer shots, especially in clutter (CuttingArmstrong2016)
example_use: customer trying frames, face and shoulders
mistakes: shooting it from 40-50 cm with a wide lens (BryanPeronaAdolphs2012: lower trust and attractiveness ratings)
definitions vary between textbooks - name the frame line (e.g. 'knees up') in prompts and shot lists
combine_with: 85-105 mm look from >= 1.2 m
how: step back, use a longer lens
limits: scale meanings are CRAFT conventions; the evidence covers reading speed and empathy, not fixed emotions

name: Close-up (CU)
camera_position: camera on the subject's axis at the distance that gives this framing
height: usually eye level unless an angle is combined
view: the face (shoulder line visible)
purpose: emotion turns, the key line, how glasses sit on the face
perceptual_effect: shot scale = size of the focal subject in the frame; smaller faces are read more slowly and need longer shots, especially in clutter (CuttingArmstrong2016)
possible_emotions: empathy if the face shows emotion (RooneyBalint2018) [EVIDENCE]
faster emotion recognition than wider scales (CuttingArmstrong2016) [EVIDENCE]
example_use: close-up of a smile when the new progressive lenses work
mistakes: close distance + wide lens (big nose, small ears); spending the CU too early (GUIDE.md)
definitions vary between textbooks - name the frame line (e.g. 'knees up') in prompts and shot lists
combine_with: shallow DOF on the near eye (85 mm f/2 at 1.5 m = ~3.5 cm DOF)
how: short durations are fine (~2.5 s typical for close scales in films)
limits: scale meanings are CRAFT conventions; the evidence covers reading speed and empathy, not fixed emotions

name: Extreme close-up (ECU)
camera_position: camera on the subject's axis at the distance that gives this framing
height: usually eye level unless an angle is combined
view: a part: eyes, mouth, a hinge (chin-to-forehead or a detail)
purpose: shock, detail, clue, sensory emphasis
perceptual_effect: shot scale = size of the focal subject in the frame; smaller faces are read more slowly and need longer shots, especially in clutter (CuttingArmstrong2016)
possible_emotions: slightly slower emotion reading at ECU than CU (CuttingArmstrong2016) [EVIDENCE, low]
example_use: an eye behind the lens with the AR-coating reflection
mistakes: DOF so thin nothing is sharp; an out-of-context ECU confuses
definitions vary between textbooks - name the frame line (e.g. 'knees up') in prompts and shot lists
combine_with: macro lighting, focus stacking for products
how: shoot as a separate insert
limits: scale meanings are CRAFT conventions; the evidence covers reading speed and empathy, not fixed emotions

name: Macro shot
camera_position: camera on the subject's axis at the distance that gives this framing
height: usually eye level unless an angle is combined
view: object at 1:2 to 1:1 magnification or closer
purpose: material truth: hinge screws, acetate layers, coating sheen
perceptual_effect: shot scale = size of the focal subject in the frame; smaller faces are read more slowly and need longer shots, especially in clutter (CuttingArmstrong2016)
example_use: acetate layer pattern and hinge rivet in a promo
mistakes: single frame at 1:1 f/11 has ~1.3 mm DOF - most of the object is soft; dust shows
definitions vary between textbooks - name the frame line (e.g. 'knees up') in prompts and shot lists
combine_with: focus stacking, long macro lens for working distance, soft gradient light for reflections
how: 100 mm macro; stack 5-10 frames
limits: scale meanings are CRAFT conventions; the evidence covers reading speed and empathy, not fixed emotions

name: Two-shot
camera_position: framing two subjects together
view: both characters in one frame
purpose: relationship, balance of power, reactions in the same frame
perceptual_effect: relative size and height in the frame are read as status [CRAFT; consistent with the verticality-power literature, Giessner2011]
possible_emotions: imbalance when one is bigger or higher [CRAFT]
example_use: Mint and Tao on a bench sharing one pair of glasses
mistakes: both centred and symmetrical with no relation
one face hidden by the other unintentionally
combine_with: staggered depth (one nearer), eyelines meeting, shared light
how: both subjects on thirds or staggered in depth
limits: meaning comes from staging

name: Group shot (three-shot and more)
camera_position: framing three or more subjects
height: eye level or slightly high so all faces show
view: several people; composed in triangles or lines
purpose: show a group, team, family or crowd dynamic
perceptual_effect: viewers find the focal person by contrast, position and the gaze of the others [CRAFT]
possible_emotions: isolation of one member placed apart [CRAFT]
example_use: shop team photo for a holiday post; a family choosing frames together
mistakes: everyone in a straight line at equal size
equal-height people at different depths with heads at different heights relative to the horizon on flat ground (perspective error, see perr.figure_horizon_mismatch)
combine_with: slight high angle to avoid hidden faces; triangular staging; one key light
how: stagger depth; run the heads-on-horizon check
limits: small faces are read slowly

name: Profile (side view)
camera_position: perpendicular to the subject's facing direction
view: pure side silhouette
purpose: show shape, the nose/temple line, walking direction, two people facing each other
perceptual_effect: the silhouette reads strongly; no eye contact with the viewer -> observer stance
possible_emotions: confrontation when two profiles face each other [CRAFT]
example_use: side view of glasses on a face showing temple length and ear fit; Mint & Tao facing each other in silhouette
mistakes: temple hides the lens shape
nose and frame edges merge with the background (no rim light)
combine_with: rim/back light for edge separation; clean background
how: camera 90 deg to the face
limits: loses the frontal lens shape

name: Three-quarter view
camera_position: ~30-45 deg off the subject's frontal axis
view: front and one side visible; the near side larger
purpose: the most dimensional standard view of faces and products
perceptual_effect: depth plus a recognisable front; for glasses shows lens shape, temple and hinge together
example_use: hero packshot of a frame at 3/4 on a mirror surface; customer turned 3/4 to the window light
mistakes: far lens not correctly foreshortened/partly hidden by the bridge; mismatched lens ellipses
temples splayed unnaturally by AI
combine_with: short lighting from the far side; 2-point perspective with distant VPs
how: turn subject or camera 30-45 deg; check ellipses (minor axis along each lens axis)
limits: needs correct ellipses and perspective

name: Front view (frontal)
camera_position: on the subject's frontal axis
view: symmetric, flat-ish; true lens shapes
purpose: show true shape (catalogue), confrontation, direct address, symmetry
perceptual_effect: direct gaze engages the viewer; symmetry reads formal/stable or uncanny
possible_emotions: formality or uncanniness with perfect symmetry [CRAFT; GUIDE.md uses it for ghosts]
example_use: catalogue front shot for spec comparison; staff talking to camera
mistakes: slight yaw making one lens bigger in a 'frontal' catalogue shot
frontal flash causing glare in the lenses
combine_with: large frontal soft light angled so reflections miss the lenses; long-lens, near-orthographic look
how: camera centred on the bridge, lens axis perpendicular to the frame front
limits: flat if lit flat

name: Rear view (from behind)
camera_position: behind the subject, facing what they face
height: subject eye height or slightly lower
view: the back of the subject plus what lies ahead (the 'Rueckenfigur')
purpose: invite the viewer to share the subject's gaze; anonymity; departure
perceptual_effect: the viewer projects into the figure; the face is hidden
possible_emotions: anonymity that suits faceless characters [DERIVED for Mint & Tao]
example_use: Mint from behind looking at the sea before deciding to book an eye test
mistakes: figure centred and blocking the view it is meant to contemplate
combine_with: figure on a third, horizon low or high, atmospheric depth ahead
how: camera behind the subject, slightly offset
limits: no facial emotion
